Proposition 11.5 uses request weights that increase rapidly with each new arrival. The theorem covers the opposite direction, including arbitrarily steep decreases. It does not prove a constant competitive ratio for arbitrary request-specific maximum penalties.

11 Lower bounds and limits of the threshold analysis

The statements in this section distinguish three different conclusions: a lower bound for all deterministic algorithms, a lower bound for the particular scaled threshold rule, and failures of that rule outside its proved delay-function assumptions. They are not interchangeable.

11.1 A deterministic problem lower bound

Theorem 11.1 (One-page deterministic lower bound).

No deterministic completing algorithm has competitive ratio strictly below two, even for one page with unit access cost and linear episode delay. The statement remains true when a fixed additive constant is allowed.

Proof.

Fix 1≤c<21\leq c<2 and any finite additive constant bb. Choose ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that δ=2−c−c​ε>0\delta=2-c-c\varepsilon>0. We construct requests one at a time. The first request arrives at a1=0a_{1}=0. Given the current finite prefix, consider the algorithm’s continuation if no further request arrives. Completion requires it to access the pending page at a finite time si≥ais_{i}\geq a_{i}. Choose the next arrival ai+1a_{i+1} strictly after sis_{i} and at most si+εs_{i}+\varepsilon. The next arrival can be chosen rational. Determinism ensures that the algorithm actually behaves as simulated through sis_{i}. After NN requests, stop the construction and let the algorithm complete the last request normally. There is no end-of-input notification.

Let τi=si−ai\tau_{i}=s_{i}-a_{i}. Each request is alone in its algorithm episode, so the algorithm pays at least ∑i=1N(1+τi)\sum_{i=1}^{N}(1+\tau_{i}). Extra accesses, if any, only increase its cost. The one-page optimum formula in Proposition 9.4 gives

OPT=1+∑i=1N−1min⁡{ai+1−ai,1}≤1+∑i=1N−1min⁡{τi+ε,1}.\operatorname{OPT}=1+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\min\{a_{i+1}-a_{i},1\}\leq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\min\{\tau_{i}+\varepsilon,1\}.

For every x≥0x\geq 0,

1+x−c​min⁡{x+ε,1}≥1+x−c​min⁡{x,1}−c​ε≥2−c−c​ε=δ.1+x-c\min\{x+\varepsilon,1\}\geq 1+x-c\min\{x,1\}-c\varepsilon\geq 2-c-c\varepsilon=\delta.

The last inequality follows separately on x≤1x\leq 1 and x≥1x\geq 1. Consequently

ALG−c​OPT≥(N−1)​δ+1−c.\operatorname{ALG}-c\operatorname{OPT}\geq(N-1)\delta+1-c.

Taking NN sufficiently large makes this exceed bb. Although the construction is adaptive, for a fixed deterministic algorithm it specifies a finite input sequence, as required for a deterministic lower bound. ∎

Theorem 11.2 (Tight deterministic guarantee for one page).

For one page of unit access cost and linear per-episode maximum delay, the algorithm that serves a pending episode exactly one time unit after its first arrival is strictly 22-competitive against the unrestricted clairvoyant optimum. Together with Theorem 11.1, the optimal deterministic competitive factor for this single-page problem is exactly 22.

Proof.

For each request at time aa, draw the interval [a,a+1][a,a+1] and let UU be their union. Consider any offline batch served at time tt, whose earliest request arrived at amina_{\min}. All the intervals of requests in the batch are contained in [amin,t+1][a_{\min},t+1]. The latter interval has length 1+t−amin1+t-a_{\min}, exactly the offline batch’s access-plus-maximum-delay cost. Taking the union across all batches and using subadditivity of length gives |U|≤OPT|U|\leq\operatorname{OPT}.

Let a1,…,aKa_{1},\ldots,a_{K} be the first arrival times of the online algorithm’s successive episodes. Each episode is cleared at aj+1a_{j}+1. The next episode begins only after that clearing, so the intervals [aj,aj+1][a_{j},a_{j}+1] have disjoint interiors and are all contained in UU. Therefore |U|≥K|U|\geq K. Each online episode costs one access plus one unit of delay, and hence ALG=2​K≤2​|U|≤2​OPT\operatorname{ALG}=2K\leq 2|U|\leq 2\operatorname{OPT}. This applies to every finite input and has no additive term. The deadline-free policy needs no signal that the input has ended. ∎

11.2 A lower bound for the scaled rank threshold

Proposition 11.3 (Reverse blocks).

For every fixed β>0\beta>0 and every m≥1m\geq 1, the scaled rank-threshold algorithm has input sequences on which its cost divided by OPT\operatorname{OPT} is at least

2​(1+β)​mm+1.\frac{2(1+\beta)m}{m+1}.

The construction can be repeated arbitrarily many times. Thus the rule’s competitive ratio uniform in mm is at least 2​(1+β)2(1+\beta), including when an instance-independent additive constant for each fixed mm is allowed. In particular, the lower bound approaches 10/310/3 at β=2/3\beta=2/3 and four at β=1\beta=1.

Proof.

Start from (1,…,m)(1,\ldots,m) and repeatedly request the block m,m−1,…,1m,m-1,\ldots,1. Separate consecutive arrivals by a fixed H>β​mH>\beta m. Each request is served before the next arrival. At every access, its page is last in the algorithm’s list, so its rank is mm, its wait is β​m\beta m, and its cost is (1+β)​m(1+\beta)m. Each block restores the initial permutation and costs (1+β)​m2(1+\beta)m^{2}.

Keeping the initial list fixed and serving every request immediately is a feasible offline schedule of cost m⁡(m+1)/2m(m+1)/2 per block. Dividing the algorithm’s cost by this feasible upper bound on OPT\operatorname{OPT} gives the displayed ratio. For any smaller proposed factor at a fixed mm, repeating blocks makes the resulting excess cost arbitrarily large, absorbing a fixed additive constant. Finally let mm grow. This is a lower bound for the specified threshold algorithm, not for all algorithms. ∎

11.3 Why the nonlinear hypotheses matter

Proposition 11.4 (Concave powers).

Let f⁡(t)=tγf(t)=t^{\gamma}, where 0<γ<10<\gamma<1. For every fixed β>0\beta>0, the rule that serves when its page’s episode penalty reaches β\beta times the current rank has unbounded competitive ratio, already on one page.

Proof.

Put τ=β1/γ\tau=\beta^{1/\gamma} and release NN requests at 0,2​τ,…,2​τ​(N−1)0,2\tau,\ldots,2\tau(N-1). The rule serves every request separately at age τ\tau, before the following arrival. Its total cost is N⁡(1+β)N(1+\beta). A feasible offline schedule serves all requests together at the final arrival, for cost

1+[2​τ​(N−1)]γ.1+[2\tau(N-1)]^{\gamma}.

The ratio of these two costs grows as Ω⁡(N1−γ)\Omega(N^{1-\gamma}), and the ratio to OPT\operatorname{OPT} is at least as large. The excess over any proposed constant multiple of the displayed comparison cost also diverges, so an additive constant does not repair the guarantee. This disproves the fixed-scale rule, not the existence of other algorithms for concave delay. ∎

Proposition 11.5 (Request-dependent linear weights).

Suppose requests to the same page may have different positive linear weights, and the delay charge of an access is the maximum weighted waiting time among the requests it clears. For every fixed β>0\beta>0, the rule that serves when this maximum reaches β\beta times the current rank has unbounded competitive ratio, even on one page.

Proof.

For i=0,…,N−1i=0,\ldots,N-1, let request ii arrive at

ai=1−4−i,wi=2​β​ 4i.a_{i}=1-4^{-i},\qquad w_{i}=2\beta\,4^{i}.

Assuming earlier requests have been cleared, its weighted age reaches β\beta at

si=ai+12⋅4i<ai+34⋅4i=ai+1s_{i}=a_{i}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 4^{i}}<a_{i}+\frac{3}{4\cdot 4^{i}}=a_{i+1}

whenever a following request exists. Inductively, every request is served alone and the algorithm pays N⁡(1+β)N(1+\beta). Offline can instead serve the entire input at time one. Every weighted age then equals wi​(1−ai)=2​βw_{i}(1-a_{i})=2\beta, so this schedule costs only 1+2​β1+2\beta. The ratio is unbounded as NN grows. Each instance is finite; the argument does not require an infinite input accumulating at time one. There is no conflict with a guarantee for a single fixed linear weight per page. ∎

11.4 A limitation of averaging the global scale

Proposition 11.6 (The existing coefficient certificate).

Choose a positive random scale BB independently of the input and run the fixed-scale rule with β=B\beta=B. Averaging the deterministic inequalities

ALGβ≤3​(1+β)​CO+2​(1+β−1)​DO\operatorname{ALG}_{\beta}\leq 3(1+\beta)C_{O}+2(1+\beta^{-1})D_{O}

cannot certify a uniform competitive factor strictly below five. This is only a limitation of these inequalities, not a randomized lower bound.

Proof.

When the two moments are finite, the averaged spatial and delay coefficients are 3​(1+𝔼​[B])3(1+\mathbb{E}[B]) and 2​(1+𝔼​[B−1])2(1+\mathbb{E}[B^{-1}]). Both would have to be strictly below five for this bound to certify a factor below five for arbitrary nonnegative CO,DOC_{O},D_{O}. That would require

𝔼⁡[B]<23,𝔼⁡[B−1]<32,\mathbb{E}[B]<\frac{2}{3},\qquad\mathbb{E}[B^{-1}]<\frac{3}{2},

contradicting 𝔼⁡[B]​𝔼​[B−1]≥1\mathbb{E}[B]\,\mathbb{E}[B^{-1}]\geq 1 by Cauchy–Schwarz. If either moment is infinite, the corresponding averaged coefficient gives no finite improvement. The deterministic choice B=2/3B=2/3 attains coefficient five. A sharper analysis of randomized scales, or an algorithm that resamples scales during its execution, is not ruled out by this argument. ∎
